source: Work Done on a Gas
W = −PΔV is the work done on the gas, and its size is the area under the path on a P–V diagram.
Students get the sign of the work wrong, mixing up the work done on the gas with the work done by it.

A gas can push a piston, so it can do work. In Work as Area Under a Force Graph work was the area under a force–distance graph. For a gas, the same idea becomes the area under a pressure–volume graph, using the gas law to connect the states.

A gas at pressure $P$ pushes on a piston of area $A$ with force $PA$. If the piston moves out a small distance $\Delta x$, the gas does work $PA\,\Delta x = P\,\Delta V$ on it. That energy leaves the gas, so the work done on the gas is $W = -P\,\Delta V$. If the pressure changes as the volume changes, add up thin strips: the size of the work is the area under the path on the P–V diagram.

Work done on a gas: $W = -P\Delta V$ at constant pressure; in general $|W|$ is the area under the path on a P–V diagram. Expansion: $W < 0$ (the gas does work). Compression: $W > 0$. Constant volume: $W = 0$. Handy: $1\,\text{kPa} \cdot \text{L} = 1\,\text{J}$.
The shaded area under the path is the size of the work; its sign depends on the direction.
Two ways of writing the same law. Since $W = -W_{\text{by}}$, they always give the same $\Delta U$.
The Energy and the First Law chapter of the Science Lab uses the work done by the gas, as in the right-hand column. Both are correct; just never mix them in one problem.
Worked examples
A gas at a constant $200\,\text{kPa}$ expands from $2.0\,\text{L}$ to $6.0\,\text{L}$. Find the work done on it.
Expanding at constant pressure
Negative: the gas did $800\,\text{J}$ of work on the piston. (Shortcut: $200\,\text{kPa} \times 4.0\,\text{L} = 800\,\text{J}$.)
A gas is compressed at a constant $150\,\text{kPa}$ from $5.0\,\text{L}$ to $2.0\,\text{L}$. Find the work done on it.
Compressing
$W = -P\Delta V = -(150\,\text{kPa})(-3.0\,\text{L}) = +450\,\text{J}$. The piston gave the gas energy.
A gas expands along a straight line on the P–V diagram from $(100\,\text{kPa}, 1.0\,\text{L})$ to $(300\,\text{kPa}, 3.0\,\text{L})$. Find the work done on it.
A sloped path
The area under a straight line is a trapezoid: $\tfrac{1}{2}(100 + 300)\,\text{kPa} \times 2.0\,\text{L} = 400\,\text{J}$.
The gas expanded, so $W = -400\,\text{J}$.

Getting the sign of the work wrong by mixing up the work done on the gas with the work done by it. Decide first: is the gas expanding (it does work, so $W$ on it is negative) or being compressed ($W$ on it is positive)? Then check that your formula agrees.
